newsitem.title: USA: Coast Guard ups restrictions on Mississippi traffic.
newsitem.headline: Coast Guard ups restrictions on Mississippi traffic.

text.p: The Coast Guard Friday added safety restrictions on Mississippi River commerce because of surging floodwaters and a dangerously fast current caused by the heaviest spring run-off in more than 60 years.

"We have never as an industry had to resort to this level of safety on the Mississippi ... (and) it is significantly slowing things down," said Ken Wells, southern area vice president of the American Waterways Operators, a Washington-based trade association representing cargo carriers.
"But there is enough concern for safety that nobody has been complaining," Wells added.

"The last time (the river) got this high was 1983 (and) the current is more difficult to deal with," said John Cascio, general manager of Moran Gulf Shipping Agencies in New Orleans, whose company handles 18 ships.
"But it would be irresponsible to shut down the river. There's so much commerce, a total shutdown would cripple a lot of people," Cascio said.

The Coast Guard ruled Friday that tank vessels or tank ships with 1,600 gross tons or more carrying certain petroleum products or chemicals, as well as deep-draft chemical tank ships, must travel in daylight hours only between mile 88 (New Orleans) and mile 233 (Baton Rouge) of the river.

A number of restrictions already in place, such as a sharp cut in tugboat loads, has cut the commercial river traffic "by a third to half" said Wells, who added that backed-up traffic at the industrial canal lock at New Orleans and elsewhere also is adding to delays.
Last Tuesday Louisiana Governor Murphy J. Foster warned large industry along the river that he might press the Coast Guard for a total shutdown of the river if he thought the population was at risk.

On Wednesday five government buildings and schools near the governor's office in Baton Rouge were evacuated after some people complained of dizziness and blurred vision. The evacuation was linked to a barge which capsized on March 17 after its tow hit the U.S. 190 bridge in Baton Rouge, spilling a liquid hydrocarbon containing toxic benzene.
A sky-blue chemical fog that intermittently has plagued local residents appeared to dissipate Friday after the barge was righted, authorities said.

Coast Guard spokesman Chris Haley told Reuters the barge was righted without incident by two cranes brought downriver from Vicksburg. "There has been vapour in the area around the barge but it hasn't spread to land," he said.

The Mississippi is one of the world's busiest waterways, with around half-a-million tons of cargo traffic a year, according to U.S. Army Corps of Engineers data. Around a quarter of that consists of oil and oil products and chemicals, the figures show.
